title: One Server, Many Hosts: The Portability Rule

questions.question: What makes it possible for one MCP server to work unchanged under two different hosts?
options: The server negotiates a private dialect separately with every host vendor
A central registry rewrites the server's tool list for each host
Every host recompiles a fresh copy of the server before connecting to it
Each host implements the same client side of one shared wire protocol
questions.explanation: Portability comes from a shared wire protocol: once a host implements the client side of the same specification version, it can drive any server that implements the matching server side, with nothing negotiated per host.

questions.question: What is a server author responsible for in an MCP deployment?
options: Building only one version that exposes its features through a shared protocol
Rendering every tool result in whatever visual style a specific host prefers
Granting the runtime permission a tool call needs before it can run
Bundling the server inside the installer package of one specific host application
questions.explanation: A server author builds and maintains one implementation against the specification itself, registering the tools, schemas, and handlers a server exposes, independent of which host or client eventually connects to it.

questions.question: Which responsibility belongs to the host rather than the server?
options: Executing the handler logic registered behind a specific tool name
Presenting a tool's result to the user in its own interface
Assigning the JSON-RPC method name that a tool call must use
Declaring the input schema attached to each tool it exposes
questions.explanation: Presentation is a host concern: the host embeds the client, receives the result payload, and decides how to show it to the person using it, while the server only produces the payload itself.

questions.question: Which of these is an operational use case MCP is built to support?
options: Encrypting network traffic between two data centers in the same region
Training a new foundation model on a company's proprietary dataset
Connecting a host to a team's internal data, tools, and workflows
Replacing a team's version control system with a new file format
questions.explanation: MCP's operational use cases are about connecting an agent host to systems a team already runs, internal data, internal tools, and internal workflows, not about replacing those systems or training new models.

questions.question: A team already uses one MCP host and now adopts a second one. What does ecosystem portability say about their existing servers?
options: Every existing server must be rewritten to match the new host exactly
The team must run two separate copies of each existing server it owns
Only servers built by the new host vendor will still keep working
The servers keep running as before since both hosts share a protocol
questions.explanation: Because both hosts implement clients against the same protocol version, an existing server keeps answering discovery and tool calls exactly as before; adopting a second host is a client-side cost, not a server rewrite.

questions.question: Two hosts call the same tool on the same server with the same arguments. Per the portability rule, what should be true of the two results?
options: The result payload is identical, though each host may present it differently
Only the first host to connect receives a valid result payload
The server returns a random result to prevent host-side caching
The payloads differ because each host negotiates its own tool schema
questions.explanation: The portability rule covers the result payload itself: identical arguments against an identical tool must return an identical result, even though two hosts are free to render that same result differently.
